grammarFocus: 名词性从句入门；that 从句；情态动词与条件表达。
title: The Library Privacy Project
instructions: 阅读下面的文章，回答10个问题。文章是关于一个模拟的图书馆隐私项目，不是真实事件。请仔细阅读，答案必须来自文章。
passage:
In the small town of Greenfield, the local library started a new project last month. The project is called 'Privacy First'. The library director, Ms. Chen, explained that the goal is to protect visitors' personal information. 'We noticed that some people were worried about their privacy,' she said. 'They asked us what we do with their data. So we decided to make some changes.'

The first change is about the computers. In the past, the library computers saved users' search history for 30 days. Now, they delete it every day. 'We think that what people search for is their own business,' Ms. Chen said. 'We don't need to keep that information.' The second change is about borrowing records. The library used to keep a list of all the books a person borrowed. Now, after a book is returned, the record is deleted after one week. 'If someone borrows a book about a personal problem, they might not want others to know,' Ms. Chen explained. 'We want to respect that.'

Not everyone agrees with the changes. Mr. Lee, a local teacher, said, 'I think that keeping records helps us understand what people like to read. If we delete everything, we won't know what books to buy.' Ms. Chen replied, 'We can still know what books are popular by looking at total numbers, not individual records. We don't need to know who borrowed what.'

The library also started a weekly workshop called 'Know Your Rights'. In the workshop, people learn how to protect their privacy online. For example, they learn that they should use strong passwords and that they should not share personal information on social media. 'Many people don't know that their data is often collected by apps,' Ms. Chen said. 'We want to help them understand what happens to their information.'

One workshop participant, a student named Anna, said, 'I didn't know that my phone apps were tracking my location. Now I turn off location services when I don't need them.' Another participant, Mr. Zhang, said, 'I learned that if I want to keep my messages private, I should use end-to-end encryption. But I also learned that nothing is 100% safe.'

The project has been running for six weeks. Ms. Chen says that about 50 people have attended the workshops. 'We are happy with the interest,' she said. 'But we still have a lot to do. Next month, we will start a new session about how to talk to children about privacy.'

What do experts say about privacy? Dr. Wang, a professor of computer science, commented, 'It is important that people understand what data they are giving away. If you use a free app, you are often paying with your data. That is something everyone should know.' She also said, 'Libraries are a good place to start this conversation because they are trusted by the community.'

The Greenfield Library plans to continue the project for at least a year. Ms. Chen hopes that other libraries will also start similar projects. 'Privacy is a basic right,' she said. 'We all need to learn how to protect it.'

In addition to the workshops, the library has made other changes to respect privacy. For example, the library now sends reminders by email instead of by phone call, because emails are less direct. Also, the library has stopped asking for visitors' home addresses when they sign up for a library card. 'We only need a name and a phone number,' Ms. Chen said. 'That is enough to contact someone.'

Another new rule is about the computers: people can now use a guest login if they do not want to use their library card number. This means that their computer use is not linked to their name. 'Some people feel safer this way,' Ms. Chen explained. 'We want everyone to feel comfortable using the library.'

The library also created a small privacy corner with books and brochures about online safety. People can take a brochure home for free. The brochures explain how to check privacy settings on social media and how to recognize phishing emails. 'We think that education is the best protection,' Ms. Chen said. 'If people know the risks, they can make better choices.'

Mr. Lee, who disagreed with some changes, agrees with the brochures. 'I think that giving people information is always good,' he said. 'My students need to know how to stay safe online. I will tell them about the privacy corner.'

So far, the project has cost very little money. The brochures were donated by a local business, and the workshops are led by volunteers. 'We are lucky to have so much support,' Ms. Chen said. 'Privacy is important for everyone, and our community is working together to protect it.'

grammar.title: 名词性从句入门：that 从句与条件表达
grammar.explanation: 英语中，that 从句可以放在某些动词（如 think, know, say, learn）后面，表示一个完整的想法。例如：'I think that keeping records helps us.' 这里的 that 可以省略，但意思不变。另外，条件句常用 if 引导，表示'如果……'，例如：'If you use a free app, you are often paying with your data.' 情态动词如 should, might, can 常用来表达建议、可能性或能力。
grammar.example: I think that keeping records helps us understand what people like to read.

options: She said that she would come.
She said that she will come.
She said that she comes.
She said that she come.
answers: She said that she would come.
questions.explanation: 在转述过去说的话时，that 从句中常用 would 表示将来。

options: If it rains, we will stay at home.
If it will rain, we stay at home.
If it rains, we stayed at home.
If it rained, we will stay at home.
answers: If it rains, we will stay at home.
questions.explanation: 条件句中，if 从句用一般现在时，主句用将来时。

options: You should protect your personal information.
You should to protect your personal information.
You should protecting your personal information.
You should protected your personal information.
answers: You should protect your personal information.
questions.explanation: 情态动词 should 后面直接跟动词原形。

options: I don't know if he will come.
I don't know if he comes.
I don't know if he came tomorrow.
I don't know if he will came.
answers: I don't know if he will come.
questions.explanation: if 可以引导宾语从句，表示'是否'，这里用将来时表示未来。
